title: S. Korea Cracks Down on Overcharging of Tourists
paragraphs: More and more foreign tourists are visiting South Korea. In the first six months of 2026, the country welcomed 10.71 million foreign visitors. But some tourists have had bad experiences, such as paying too much for taxis and hotels. Now, the South Korean government is taking strong action against businesses that overcharge tourists.

In February 2026, President Lee Jae Myung said that the government wants tourists to come back to Korea again and again. To do this, the government announced new measures against unfair prices. According to the government, the most common complaint from foreign visitors was about taxi fares that were too high. The second most common complaint was about hotels and other places to stay, especially during concerts by popular K-pop groups.

For example, before a BTS concert in Busan in June, the average price of a hotel room in the city was already 2.4 times higher than normal. Some small hotels raised their prices from 100,000 won to as much as 750,000 won per night. Some hotels even canceled bookings and then offered the same rooms again at higher prices.

Under the new rules, taxi drivers who overcharge passengers will lose their license for 30 days, even for a first mistake. Drivers who overcharge three times may lose their license permanently. In addition, from August 4, 2026, guesthouses and traditional Korean houses that overcharge or do not show their prices will have to close for five days, even for a first offense. Street food stalls will also have to show their prices clearly.
Government officials said that "Fair pricing is fundamental to building lasting trust with travelers."
The government hopes these measures will help it reach its goal of 23 million foreign visitors in 2026. In 2025, there were 18.94 million.
However, critics say the rules must be enforced. In Seoul, only about 3% of taxi complaints by foreign passengers between 2021 and August 2026 led to penalties.
